boundaries: the sealed envelope every client must read
the shared vectors, computed by Node

instruments.evidence: G2a: a sibling vector generator, the vectors, groupKeys.ts and its tests. A group has one AES-256-GCM key per numbered version, wrapped per member with RSA-OAEP and never held by the server.

6febb92fc, 8bc3efc78 and d67e47c15, the three ledgers for the login-key vectors. 6febb92fc set the standard this pass had to meet: B5 recorded as running the real WebCrypto derivation against a separate implementation's values, not a restatement of its own output.

Printed the vectors themselves and read them: two sealed envelopes, versions 1 and 7, each ciphertext plus a 16-byte GCM tag. Version 7 carries multi-byte text, so they pin UTF-8 encoding and not only the cipher.

instruments.why: No markup; this is a crypto module with no rendered output.
No HTTP body; the service that speaks to the key routes is G2b and is unwritten.
No stored row; the server holds only wrapped copies, and nothing here writes them yet.

instruments.evidence: The envelope is the seam: {v,k,iv,data}. The module reads and writes the same shape the generator emits, and the test asserts the whole envelope rather than the ciphertext alone.
The caller receives a JSON string and gets the key version back without opening it, which is what a reader needs to choose a key.

The finding. Two implementations, but the differential ran in one direction only: the tests proved WebCrypto opens what Node sealed and nothing proved it produces what Node produced, because sealGroupMessage draws a fresh IV and can never be compared to a fixed vector.

instruments.why: No worker or provider; the vectors are generated by hand and committed, as login-keys.json is.

instruments.evidence: The key version is wired, not decorative: sealedKeyVersion reads it back from a real envelope, and the vectors carry two different versions so the field cannot be hardcoded.

instruments.why: No untyped accessor.

instruments.evidence: The fixture is a separate implementation. Node's crypto sealed the vectors, so matching them cannot be self-confirmation the way a WebCrypto-generated fixture would be.
Real inputs that must pass: both vectors open, the key version survives, a member copy round-trips a real RSA key pair.
Inputs that must fail: four malformed envelopes (wrong version, wrong types, missing field) are all refused, and a message will not open under another key.
Two materially different inputs along the dimension the code branches on: version 1 is pure ASCII, version 7 carries combining characters. That difference is what the control later turned on.

Compared against the sibling scheme: loginKeys.ts wraps one secret under a derived key, this wraps one shared key per member. Both use a versioned JSON envelope and both import the same base64 helpers.
No unreachable branch: every export is exercised, and the module has no production consumer yet, so nothing is dead by accident rather than by design.
Nothing is swallowed. A member whose published key will not import is reported as unusable rather than skipped, because a member dropped from the copies is a member who cannot read the group.

instruments.why: No flag.

instruments.evidence: The generator is a sibling of generate.mjs rather than a second mode of it: three consumers read login-keys.json by name, so that script's one documented redirect had to keep producing exactly what it produces.
Shape 'a client that cannot read what another client writes': the reason the one-directional pin matters. A sealing divergence would round-trip through openGroupMessage and pass every other test.

instruments.why: No concurrency; the module is pure crypto over its arguments.
No transaction.
No migration.
No delete, cancel or orphan path.

instruments.evidence: Control built for the finding, and building it is what exposed that the first fix was blind; see the finding and pass 2.
The guard is reachable: wrapGroupKeyForMembers reports both an absent key and an unreadable one, each driven by its own test.
Prettier clean, ESLint clean, and a type checker proven rather than trusted: a deliberate type error was introduced, tsc caught it at groupKeys.ts(163,7), and the file was restored.
No new instrument. C3 names this exactly, and the gap was that the differential it describes had been run in one direction.

Applied, and it is the whole point of the phase. Ran the real WebCrypto side against vectors a separate implementation produced: all vector cases open, and sealing deterministically with each vector's own IV yields byte-identical base64, printed side by side for both versions.

instruments.why: Nothing starts before its governing decision.

instruments.evidence: Fed the guard what it exists to refuse: an empty published key and a malformed one, each reported with its own reason rather than thrown or skipped.

findings.summary: The vectors were pinned in one direction only: the tests proved WebCrypto opens what Node sealed, and nothing proved it produces what Node produced, because sealGroupMessage draws a fresh IV and so can never be compared to a fixed vector. A change that made this client's ciphertext diverge would round-trip through openGroupMessage, pass every test, and leave no other client able to read what it writes. The first fix was itself blind -- it called window.crypto directly instead of the module, so no mutation of groupKeys.ts could fail it -- which building the control exposed.

control.observed: With the encoding mutated to NFD inside the seam, twelve tests pass and one fails with a real AssertionError: 'produces the same envelope Node did for version 7'. Version 1 is pure ASCII and unaffected, so the control also shows why the multi-byte vector is there.

instruments.evidence: The fix from pass 1 plus its correction: sealGroupMessage now delegates to sealGroupMessageWithIv, and the test seals through the module rather than around it.
